claim: Enzalutamide was recently approved for patients with castration-resistant prostate cancer.
source: The second-generation antiandrogen enzalutamide was recently approved for patients with castration-resistant prostate cancer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by the FDA approval mentioned in the introduction (Tran et al., 2009; Scher et al., 2012).

claim: The duration of response to enzalutamide is often limited.
source: Despite its success, the duration of response is often limited.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about enzalutamide treatment.

claim: One mechanism of resistance to previous antiandrogens is mutation of the androgen receptor (AR).
source: For previous antiandrogens, one mechanism of resistance is mutation of the androgen receptor (AR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Bergerat and Ceraline, 2009).

claim: A reporter-based mutagenesis screen identified a novel mutation, F876L, which converted enzalutamide into an AR agonist.
source: To prospectively identify AR mutations that might confer resistance to enzalutamide, we performed a reporter-based mutagenesis screen and identified a novel mutation, F876L, which converted enzalutamide into an AR agonist.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Ectopic expression of AR F876L rescued the growth inhibition of enzalutamide treatment.
source: Ectopic expression of AR F876L rescued the growth inhibition of enzalutamide treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by growth assay data in Figure 2D, E, and F.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations suggested a mechanism by which the F876L substitution alleviates antagonism through repositioning of the coactivator recruiting helix 12.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations performed on antiandrogen–AR complexes suggested a mechanism by which the F876L substitution alleviates antagonism through repositioning of the coactivator recruiting helix 12.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Three novel compounds were identified that effectively antagonized AR F876L (and AR WT) to suppress the growth of prostate cancer cells resistant to enzalutamide.
source: This model then provided the rationale for a focused chemical screen which, based on existing antiandrogen scaffolds, identified three novel compounds that effectively antagonized AR F876L (and AR WT) to suppress the growth of prostate cancer cells resistant to enzalutamide.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Reactivation of AR signaling has been implicated in resistance to previous antiandrogen therapy.
source: Reactivation of AR signaling has been implicated in resistance to previous antiandrogen therapy (Linja et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Point mutation in the ligand-binding domain (LBD) of AR is one well-documented mechanism of reactivation.
source: and one well-documented mechanism of reactivation is point mutation in the ligand-binding domain (LBD) of AR (Bergerat and Ceraline, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Many AR mutations broaden ligand specificity.
source: Many of these mutations broaden ligand specificity
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Some AR mutations confer resistance by converting the AR antagonist into an agonist of the mutant receptor.
source: and some confer resistance by converting the AR antagonist into an agonist of the mutant receptor (Veldscholte et al., 1990; Haapala et al., 2001; Hara et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Unbiased mutagenesis screens in preclinical models can identify a priori clinically relevant mutations that alter drug activity.
source: Because previous work with targeted therapies that inhibit oncogenic kinases has shown that unbiased mutagenesis screens in preclinical models can identify a priori clinically relevant mutations that alter drug activity (Azam et al., 2003; Burgess et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: An AR-regulated EGFP reporter with a probasin promoter and PSA enhancer elements was used to screen for and enrich cell populations bearing biologically active mutations.
source: To this end, an AR-regulated EGFP reporter, with a probasin promoter and PSA enhancer elements driving EGFP expression (Pb.PSE.EGFP) (Chapel-Fernandes et al., 2006), was used to screen for and enrich cell populations bearing biologically active mutations (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Proof-of-concept studies were conducted with LNCaP cells cotransduced with Pb.PSE.EGFP and AR W741C.
source: Proof-of-concept studies were conducted with LNCaP cells cotransduced with Pb.PSE.EGFP and AR W741C, a well-characterized mutation that converts the AR antagonist bicalutamide into an agonist (Haapala et al., 2001; Hara et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: AR W741C is a well-characterized mutation that converts the AR antagonist bicalutamide into an agonist.
source: AR W741C, a well-characterized mutation that converts the AR antagonist bicalutamide into an agonist (Haapala et al., 2001; Hara et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: After four rounds of bicalutamide 'selection' and sorting, LNCaP cells expressing AR W741C dominated the final populations.
source: After four rounds of bicalutamide 'selection' and sorting, LNCaP cells expressing AR W741C dominated the final populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: After five iterations of enzalutamide exposure and FACS sorting, a population of cells with durable EGFP expression was identified.
source: After five iterations of enzalutamide exposure and FACS sorting, we identified a population of cells with durable EGFP expression (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: Enzalutamide promoted AR transcriptional activity in the enriched cell population, reflected by induction of EGFP expression compared to vehicle control.
source: Moreover, enzalutamide promoted AR transcriptional activity in these cells, reflected by induction of EGFP expression compared to vehicle control (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: Analysis of endogenous AR target gene expression confirmed that enzalutamide behaved as an agonist in the enriched cell population.
source: Analysis of endogenous AR target gene expression confirmed that enzalutamide behaved as an agonist in the enriched cell population (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: siRNA knockdown of AR showed that pharmacologically induced changes remained AR dependent.
source: and siRNA knockdown of AR showed that these pharmacologically induced changes remained AR dependent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: In two of three replicates, a single dominant point mutation emerged, resulting in the amino acid substitution F876L.
source: In two of three replicates, a single dominant point mutation emerged, resulting in the amino acid substitution F876L (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequencing data in Figure 1C.

claim: The F876L mutation clearly enriched throughout the selection process.
source: Importantly, this mutation clearly enriched throughout the selection process (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Treatment of LNCaP-Pb.PSE.EGFP cells expressing AR F876L with enzalutamide resulted in a dose-dependent induction of EGFP expression.
source: Treatment of these cells with enzalutamide resulted in a dose-dependent induction of EGFP expression (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Enzalutamide treatment induced luciferase activity ∼50-fold in AR-negative CV1 cells expressing AR F876L with an AR-dependent luciferase construct.
source: We also introduced AR F876L cDNA into AR-negative CV1 cells along with an AR-dependent luciferase construct, and upon enzalutamide treatment, luciferase activity was induced ∼50-fold (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: The results with AR F876L were comparable to those seen with the previously reported AR mutations T877A and W741C.
source: These results were comparable to those seen with the previously reported AR mutations T877A and W741C, which confer agonism to hydroxyflutamide and bicalutamide, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Enzalutamide treatment potently induced nuclear localization of AR F876L.
source: Moreover, enzalutamide treatment potently induced nuclear localization of AR F876L (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation studies showed that enzalutamide recruited AR F876L to the enhancers of AR target genes.
source: and chromatin immunoprecipitation studies showed that enzalutamide recruited AR F876L to the enhancers of AR target genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by ChIP data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Endogenous AR target gene expression was either no longer repressed by enzalutamide or strongly induced by enzalutamide in cells expressing AR F876L.
source: Consistent with these results, endogenous AR target gene expression was either no longer repressed by enzalutamide (Figure 2C, left) or strongly induced by enzalutamide in cells expressing AR F876L (Figure 2C, right).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2C.

claim: Enzalutamide binds with higher affinity to AR F876L than wild-type AR.
source: A competition assay with 16β[18F]fluoro-5α-DHT (18F-FDHT), to measure relative AR binding affinity (Tran et al., 2009), showed that enzalutamide binds with higher affinity to AR F876L than wild-type AR (Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by binding assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: F876L similarly impacted the pharmacology of ARN-509, a structurally discrete antiandrogen sharing the bisaryl-thiohydantoin core motif.
source: Notably, F876L similarly impacted the pharmacology of ARN-509 (Clegg et al., 2012), a structurally discrete antiandrogen sharing the bisaryl-thiohydantoin core motif (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplements 4, 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplements 4, 5.

claim: Overexpression of AR F876L in VCaP cells entirely reversed the growth inhibition phenotype caused by enzalutamide treatment.
source: Although enzalutamide treatment potently inhibits the growth of parental VCaP cells (Tran et al., 2009), overexpression of AR F876L entirely reversed this phenotype (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 2D.

claim: Enzalutamide rescued the growth of VCaP/AR F876L cells in androgen-depleted media, similar to that seen with the endogenous androgen DHT.
source: Enzalutamide also rescued the growth of VCaP/AR F876L cells in androgen-depleted media, similar to that seen with the endogenous androgen DHT (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 2E.

claim: The growth inhibition results were recapitulated in CWR22Pc cells, another prostate cancer cell line that is sensitive to enzalutamide.
source: Finally, these results were recapitulated in CWR22Pc cells, another prostate cancer cell line that is sensitive to enzalutamide (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A,B.

claim: The growth of wild-type AR tumors was almost completely inhibited by enzalutamide treatment in vivo.
source: While the growth of wild-type AR tumors was almost completely inhibited by enzalutamide treatment, tumors expressing AR F876L grew rapidly in the presence of enzalutamide, similar to vehicle-treated tumors of either genotype (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by xenograft data in Figure 2F.

claim: Tumors expressing AR F876L grew rapidly in the presence of enzalutamide, similar to vehicle-treated tumors of either genotype.
source: While the growth of wild-type AR tumors was almost completely inhibited by enzalutamide treatment, tumors expressing AR F876L grew rapidly in the presence of enzalutamide, similar to vehicle-treated tumors of either genotype (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by xenograft data in Figure 2F.

claim: After culturing CWR22Pc cells in vitro with enzalutamide for several months, more than 50% of the cells expressed the F876L mutation.
source: After culturing CWR22Pc cells in vitro with enzalutamide for several months, more than 50% of the cells expressed the F876L mutation (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by deep sequencing data in Table 1.

claim: Prolonged culture of CWR22Pc cells with ARN-509 selected for a small population (∼1.3%) expressing AR F876L.
source: Prolonged culture of these cells with ARN-509 also selected for a small population (∼1.3%) expressing AR F876L.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by deep sequencing data in Table 1.

claim: Long-term enzalutamide or ARN-509 therapy in mice bearing LNCaP/AR xenograft tumors resulted in the outgrowth of tumor cell populations expressing AR F876L.
source: In vivo, long-term enzalutamide or ARN-509 therapy in mice bearing LNCaP/AR xenograft tumors also resulted in the outgrowth of tumor cell populations expressing AR F876L (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by deep sequencing data in Table 1.

claim: AR F876L predominated in one tumor (∼71%), was present at low frequency in four other tumors (∼1 to 2%), and a distinct amino acid substitution at this residue, F876I, was enriched in one enzalutamide-resistant tumor.
source: Sequencing revealed that AR F876L predominated in one tumor (∼71%), was present at low frequency in four other tumors (∼1 to 2%), and that a distinct amino acid substitution at this residue, F876I, was enriched in one enzalutamide-resistant tumor (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by deep sequencing data in Table 2.

claim: A conservative F876Y substitution did not alter the pharmacology of enzalutamide or ARN-509.
source: A conservative F876Y substitution did not alter the pharmacology of either drug, but aliphatic substitutions structurally similar to F876L, such as F876I (also found in one xenograft with acquired resistance), conferred agonism to both enzalutamide and ARN-509 (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: Aliphatic substitutions structurally similar to F876L, such as F876I, conferred agonism to both enzalutamide and ARN-509.
source: A conservative F876Y substitution did not alter the pharmacology of either drug, but aliphatic substitutions structurally similar to F876L, such as F876I (also found in one xenograft with acquired resistance), conferred agonism to both enzalutamide and ARN-509 (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: Bicalutamide did not induce AR F876L transcriptional activity in the luciferase reporter assay, either at low or at high concentrations.
source: Notably, we observed that bicalutamide did not induce AR F876L transcriptional activity in our luciferase reporter assay, either at low (Figure 2B) or at high (Figure 2—figure supplement 7) concentrations
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: Bicalutamide retains weak antagonist activity against AR F876L.
source: suggesting that it retains weak antagonist activity against this mutant.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bicalutamide does not induce AR F876L activity.

claim: While at low doses, bicalutamide is an effective inhibitor of AR F876L, it loses potency at higher concentrations.
source: We conducted EGFP reporter assays to determine if AR F876L transcriptional activity is inhibited by bicalutamide, and found that while at low doses, it is an effective inhibitor of AR F876L, it loses potency at higher concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by EGFP reporter assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: Only minimal growth inhibition was observed in CWR22Pc cells expressing AR F876L with bicalutamide treatment.
source: We also observed only minimal growth inhibition in CWR22Pc cells expressing AR F876L with bicalutamide treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A.

claim: AR overexpression is a common resistance mechanism in patients with CRPC.
source: These data, along with the knowledge that AR overexpression is a common resistance mechanism in patients with CRPC (Linja et al., 2001)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: AR overexpression confers partial agonism on bicalutamide.
source: and confers partial agonism on bicalutamide (Chen et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Bicalutamide is not a viable treatment option for patients who fail on enzalutamide due to AR F876L mutation.
source: suggest that bicalutamide is not a viable treatment option for patients who fail on enzalutamide due to AR F876L mutation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing bicalutamide's limited efficacy against AR F876L.

claim: Both enzalutamide and ARN-509 share identical A-rings with bicalutamide.
source: In designing the study, we noted that both enzalutamide and ARN-509 share identical A-rings with bicalutamide (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Bicalutamide and its derivative S1 were respectively cocrystallized with the LBD of AR W741L and AR WT in agonist conformations.
source: and its derivative S1 that were respectively cocrystallized with the LBD of AR W741L and AR WT in agonist conformations (PDB ID 1Z95 and 2AXA) (Bohl et al., 2005a, 2005b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: 2AXA was chosen as a structural template as it bears fewer amino acid substitutions compared to 1Z95.
source: 2AXA was chosen as a structural template as it bears fewer amino acid substitutions compared to 1Z95.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological choice.

claim: The docked enzalutamide and ARN-509 molecules demonstrated strikingly different interaction patterns with AR compared to bicalutamide.
source: The docked enzalutamide and ARN-509 molecules demonstrated strikingly different interaction patterns with AR compared to bicalutamide (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The thiohydantoin B-ring prevents enzalutamide and ARN-509 from accessing the 'H12 pocket' occupied by bicalutamide.
source: Notably, the thiohydantoin B-ring prevents the compound from accessing the 'H12 pocket' occupied by bicalutamide.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulation results.

claim: The conformationally restricted thiohydantoin forces the C-ring to bind a region near the C terminus of helix 11 and the loop connecting helices 11 and 12, termed the 'H11 pocket'.
source: Instead, the conformationally restricted thiohydantoin forces the C-ring to bind a region near the C terminus of helix 11 and the loop connecting helices 11 and 12, that we termed the 'H11 pocket'.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulation results.

claim: Accommodation of the C-ring in the H11 pocket is coupled to significant conformational rearrangements of residues on H11 and the H11–H12 connecting loop that prevents H12 from adopting the agonist conformation required for efficient coactivator recruitment.
source: As seen in the MD simulations using the WT receptor with enzalutamide and ARN-509 (Figure 3D,E [in red], Figure 3—figure supplement 1), accommodation of the C-ring in this region is coupled to significant conformational rearrangements of residues on H11 and the H11–H12 connecting loop that prevents H12 from adopting the agonist conformation required for efficient coactivator recruitment.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 3D,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: For WT receptors in complex with enzalutamide and ARN-509, the average RMSDs to the crystal agonist conformation for the helix 11 terminus (residues 875–882) were measured at 2.24 and 1.94 Å, respectively.
source: For WT receptors in complex with enzalutamide and ARN-509, the average RMSDs to the crystal agonist conformation for the helix 11 terminus (residues 875–882) were measured at 2.24 and 1.94 Å, respectively
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulation analysis.

claim: For WT receptors in complex with enzalutamide and ARN-509, the average RMSDs for the helix 12 terminus (residues 893–900) were 1.81 and 2.08 Å, respectively.
source: and those for the helix 12 terminus (residues 893–900) were 1.81 and 2.08 Å, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulation analysis.

claim: For the F876L mutants, the average RMSDs for helix 11 were somewhat lower at 1.01 and 1.70 Å for enzalutamide and ARN-509, respectively.
source: For the F876L mutants, in comparison, the average RMSDs for helix 11 were somewhat lower at 1.01 and 1.70 Å for enzalutamide and ARN-509, respectively
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulation analysis.

claim: For the F876L mutants, the average RMSDs for helix 12 went down to 1.37 Å for both enzalutamide and ARN-509.
source: and those for helix 12 went down to 1.37 Å for both ligands.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulation analysis.

claim: The F876L mutation allows the receptor to reposition H12 in a more agonist-like conformation that is compatible with coactivator recruitment.
source: The results demonstrate that despite inducing similar dislocations in the H11 pocket, the mutation allows the receptor to reposition H12 in a more agonist-like conformation that is compatible with coactivator recruitment (Figure 3D,E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 3D,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: F876 in AR WT likely interacts with the C-ring end of enzalutamide or ARN-509 through favorable pi stacking or van der Waals contacts.
source: A close look in the H11 pocket (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B) indicated the following: (1) F876 in AR WT likely interacts with the C-ring end of enzalutamide or ARN-509 through favorable pi stacking or van der Waals contacts
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The loss of favorable contacts upon F876L mutation concurrently affects the conformational choices of helices 11 and 12, which interact through both bonded and nonbonded forces.
source: and (2) the loss of such favorable contacts upon F876L mutation concurrently affects the conformational choices of helices 11 and 12, which interact through both bonded and nonbonded forces.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulation analysis.

claim: The structural modeling results are consistent with the differential resistance profiles for enzalutamide and bicalutamide involving residues 741 and 876, respectively.
source: Importantly, these structural modeling results are consistent with the differential resistance profiles for enzalutamide and bicalutamide involving residues 741 and 876, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: The substituent on position 4 of the B-ring was predicted to lie in close proximity to residues on H12 of the mutant receptor.
source: Another notable insight from these simulations was that the substituent on position 4 of the B-ring (i.e., the geminal [gem]-dimethyl group on enzalutamide, the spirocyclobutyl ring on ARN-509; Figure 4A) was predicted to lie in close proximity to residues on H12 of the mutant receptor (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 3D,E and Figure 4A.

claim: The steric girth of the substituent appeared to impact the positioning of H12, as the bulkier spirocyclobutyl moiety on ARN-509 elicited greater H12 displacements in AR WT than did enzalutamide's gem-dimethyl group.
source: Moreover, the steric girth of the substituent appeared to impact the positioning of H12, as the bulkier spirocyclobutyl moiety on ARN-509 elicited greater H12 displacements in AR WT than did enzalutamide's gem-dimethyl group (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 3E.

claim: A series of analogues bearing saturated hydrocarbon spirocycles of incrementally greater size and complexity on the B-ring of the enzalutamide scaffold (DR100-103) were designed and synthesized.
source: To restore the positioning of H12 into an antagonist conformation for AR F876L, we designed and synthesized a series of analogues bearing saturated hydrocarbon spirocycles of incrementally greater size and complexity on the B-ring of the enzalutamide scaffold (DR100-103, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: The DR100-103 series inhibited the transcriptional activity of AR WT in the EGFP reporter assay.
source: Consistent with this precedent, the DR100-103 series inhibited the transcriptional activity of AR WT in the EGFP reporter assay (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by EGFP reporter assay data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: DR100-102 behaved as strong agonists for AR F876L.
source: Whereas DR100-102 behaved as strong agonists for AR F876L (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by EGFP reporter assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: (±)-DR103 potently inhibited the mutant AR F876L receptor and antagonized DHT induction.
source: (±)-DR103 potently inhibited the mutant receptor and antagonized DHT induction (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by EGFP reporter and luciferase assay data in Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: (±)-DR103 was a more potent inhibitor of AR F876L than AR WT.
source: We also found that (±)-DR103 was a more potent inhibitor of AR F876L than AR WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: A compound with the gem-dimethyl group on position 4 (rather than 3/5) of the D-ring (DR104) was a modest agonist of AR F876L (albeit an antagonist of AR WT).
source: Remarkably, a compound with the gem-dimethyl group on position 4 (rather than 3/5) of the D-ring (DR104) was a modest agonist of AR F876L (albeit an antagonist of AR WT).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by EGFP reporter assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A compound with gem-dimethyl groups at the 3 and 5 positions of the D-ring (DR105) inhibited AR F876L (and AR WT).
source: Moreover, a compound with gem-dimethyl groups at the 3 and 5 positions of the D-ring (DR105) inhibited AR F876L (and AR WT) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by EGFP reporter assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Transplanting the D-ring from (±)-DR103 onto the ARN-509 scaffold ([±]-DR106) resulted in AR F876L inhibition.
source: Encouragingly, transplanting the D-ring from (±)-DR103 onto the ARN-509 scaffold ([±]-DR106) also resulted in AR F876L inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by EGFP reporter assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DR107, a compound built on the enzalutamide scaffold bearing only hydrogen atoms at position 4 on the B-ring, was an agonist both for AR WT and AR F876L.
source: Finally, to underscore the importance of the steric interactions conferred by the D-ring, we synthesized DR107, a compound built on the enzalutamide scaffold bearing only hydrogen atoms at position 4 on the B-ring. This molecule was an agonist both for AR WT and AR F876L (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by EGFP reporter assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: (±)-DR103 inhibited the growth of prostate cancer cell lines expressing both the WT and mutant receptor.
source: In line with this pharmacology, (±)-DR103 inhibited the growth of prostate cancer cell lines expressing both the WT and mutant receptor (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: DR101, a close structural analogue that behaved as an agonist for AR F876L, did not inhibit cell growth at equivalent doses.
source: DR101, a close structural analogue that behaved as an agonist for AR F876L, did not inhibit cell growth at equivalent doses (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 4B.

claim: The dose of (±)-DR103 required to observe antiproliferative effects (10 μM) did not impact the growth of DU145 (an AR-null human prostate cancer cell line), supporting the specificity of the antiandrogen.
source: Finally, the dose of (±)-DR103 required to observe antiproliferative effects (10 μM) did not impact the growth of DU145 (an AR-null human prostate cancer cell line), supporting the specificity of the antiandrogen (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: MD simulations using (S)-DR103 suggested that an agonist-like conformation of H12 cannot be achieved for either WT or mutant AR.
source: Unlike the results for enzalutamide and ARN-509, MD simulations using (S)-DR103 suggested that an agonist-like conformation of H12 cannot be achieved for either WT or mutant AR (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: The D-ring on (S)-DR103 was capable of directly displacing the N-terminal residues of H12.
source: The modeling study instead showed that the D-ring on (S)-DR103 was capable of directly displacing the N-terminal residues of H12.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MD simulation analysis.

claim: (S)-DR103 occupies a region in the H12 pocket that neither enzalutamide nor ARN-509 can access, thus imposing antagonist-like dislocation of helix 12.
source: A magnified view of the H12 pocket (Figure 4—figure supplement 8) shows that (S)-DR103 occupies a region in the H12 pocket that neither enzalutamide nor ARN-509 can access, thus imposing antagonist-like dislocation of helix 12.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: (S)-DR103 did not show a significant difference in binding with residue L876 compared to either enzalutamide or ARN-509 in the H11 pocket.
source: Whereas in the H11 pocket (Figure 4—figure supplement 8), (S)-DR103 did not show a significant difference in binding with residue L876 compared to either enzalutamide or ARN-509
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: The restored antagonism by (S)-DR103 was not achieved by simply regaining interactions at the mutation site in AR.
source: which suggests that the restored antagonism was not achieved by simply regaining interactions at the mutation site in AR.
evidence: This is inferred from the MD simulation analysis showing similar binding in the H11 pocket.

claim: MD simulations for the complex of AR F876L and (R)-DR103 showed a slightly less pronounced H12 dislocation compared to (S)-DR103.
source: Similar MD simulations for the complex of AR F876L and (R)-DR103 showed a slightly less pronounced H12 dislocation (Figure 4—figure supplement 7)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: The two enantiomers of DR103 might cause different levels of antagonism.
source: suggesting that the two enantiomers might cause different levels of antagonism.
evidence: This is inferred from the MD simulation results showing different H12 dislocations.

claim: Understanding mechanisms of drug resistance is a crucial first step in developing strategies to prevent or overcome it.
source: As is evident from previous work with ABL kinase inhibitors for chronic myeloid leukemia and antivirals for HIV and hepatitis (Shah et al., 2004; Glickman and Sawyers, 2012), understanding mechanisms of drug resistance is a crucial first step in developing strategies to prevent or overcome it.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: AR mutations are a cause of clinical resistance to antiandrogens (flutamide and bicalutamide).
source: Because AR mutations are a cause of clinical resistance to antiandrogens (flutamide and bicalutamide) (Veldscholte et al., 1990; Haapala et al., 2001)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Clinically relevant mutations can be discovered from screening platforms in preclinical models.
source: and previous work has shown that clinically relevant mutations can be discovered from screening platforms in preclinical models
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as established knowledge.

claim: The F876L mutation was recovered 'spontaneously' from enzalutamide-sensitive cell line and xenograft models treated with prolonged enzalutamide therapy.
source: Importantly, this mutation was also recovered 'spontaneously' from enzalutamide-sensitive cell line and xenograft models treated with prolonged enzalutamide therapy.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Prostate cancer can spontaneously acquire gain-of-function mutations in AR rather than acquiring mutations that simply preclude inhibitor binding.
source: That prostate cancer can spontaneously acquire gain-of-function mutations in AR (rather than acquiring mutations that simply preclude inhibitor binding) underscores the special challenge in pharmacologically overcoming this mechanism of resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: A single amino acid can determine sensitivity to RU486 in the progesterone receptor.
source: By borrowing insight from studies of the progesterone receptor, showing that a single amino acid can determine sensitivity to RU486, and structural analyses of the estrogen receptor (Benhamou et al., 1992; Shiau et al., 1998)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The MD simulations argued that an altered spatial orientation of enzalutamide within the AR LBD might explain the onset of agonism, as the F876L mutation appeared to reposition the drug to eliminate steric clashes that promoted H12 dislocation in AR WT.
source: More importantly, the MD simulations argued that an altered spatial orientation of enzalutamide within the AR LBD might explain the onset of agonism, as the F876L mutation appeared to reposition the drug to eliminate steric clashes that promoted H12 dislocation in AR WT.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the MD simulation results.

claim: Several larger compounds that the MD simulations predicted could restore H12 dislocation (the 'D-ring' series) effectively antagonized AR F876L.
source: Reassuringly, several larger compounds that the MD simulations predicted could restore H12 dislocation (the 'D-ring' series) effectively antagonized AR F876L.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: It is difficult to envision how the importance of the D-ring might have otherwise emerged from previous (and ongoing) chemical screening efforts without the discovery of the F876L mutation and its companion pharmacology.
source: Because the discovery of this mutation and its companion pharmacology provided the basis for our structural model, it is difficult to envision how the importance of the D-ring might have otherwise emerged from previous (and ongoing) chemical screening efforts.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Among the ∼100 bisaryl-thiohydantoins published to date, several compounds bearing structurally similar moieties to the bioactive series were essentially indistinguishable from enzalutamide, ARN-509, or other leading agents in conventional cell-based assays.
source: Among the ∼100 bisaryl-thiohydantoins published to date, several compounds bearing structurally similar moieties to our bioactive series were essentially indistinguishable from enzalutamide, ARN-509, or other leading agents in conventional cell-based assays.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as context for the findings.

claim: The focused chemical screen further speaks to the unusually complicated pharmacobiology of AR F876L, as subtle changes in the position of geminal dimethyl moieties on DR103-5 radically impacted the respective bioactivity of the drugs.
source: Our own focused chemical screen further speaks to the unusually complicated pharmacobiology of AR F876L, as subtle changes in the position of geminal dimethyl moieties on DR103-5 radically impacted the respective bioactivity of the drugs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Success in predicting the pharmacology of candidate inhibitors with MD simulations argues for a novel workflow by which in silico screening could guide future antiandrogen drug discovery.
source: Our success predicting the pharmacology of candidate inhibitors with MD simulations argues for a novel workflow by which in silico screening could guide future antiandrogen drug discovery (pending a cocrystal structure of an AR/antagonist complex).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: ∼50% of patients fail to respond to enzalutamide.
source: The data indicating that ∼50% of patients fail to respond to enzalutamide has somewhat overshadowed the importance of the discovery of the bisaryl-thiohydantoin chemotype for AR
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as context.

claim: The structural model provides a powerful tool to further refine the bisaryl-thiohydantoin chemotype into drug candidates with improved properties.
source: In this regard, our structural model provides a powerful tool to further refine the chemotype into drug candidates with improved properties.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Discovery of the AR F876L mutation will facilitate solution of the enzalutamide/AR complex by X-ray crystallography.
source: We are optimistic that discovery of the AR F876L mutation will facilitate solution of the enzalutamide/AR complex by X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation about future work.

claim: Within 2 years of reporting dasatinib-resistant mutations in BCR-ABL in a preclinical model, analogous mutations were recovered from dasatinib-resistant chronic myeloid leukemia patients.
source: As for the potential clinical impact of a priori discovery of drug–resistance mutations to novel cancer drugs, our previous experience with the ABL kinase inhibitor dasatinib in chronic myeloid leukemia serves as an example. Within 2 years of reporting dasatinib-resistant mutations in BCR-ABL in a preclinical model, analogous mutations were recovered from dasatinib-resistant chronic myeloid leukemia patients (Burgess et al., 2005; Shah et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Routine rebiopsy of tumor tissue in men with castration-resistant prostate cancer is challenging due to the high frequency of osteoblastic bone lesions consisting primarily of stromal tissue.
source: Routine rebiopsy of tumor tissue in men with castration-resistant prostate cancer is challenging due to the high frequency of osteoblastic bone lesions consisting primarily of stromal tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as context for clinical application.

claim: Blood-based assays for AR mutation detection may be a compelling alternative, based on recent success in detection of tumor-specific mutations in circulating plasma DNA from patients with other cancers.
source: Blood-based assays for AR mutation detection may be a compelling alternative, based on recent success in detection of tumor-specific mutations in circulating plasma DNA from patients with other cancers (Diehl et al., 2008; Leary et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.
